rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all six compounds and identify critical pairs while targeting a last peak near 10 minutes. The retention pattern will guide trimming the solvent window and testing slope or temperature.

Injection 1 already achieves the maximum CRF. Shorten the gradient while holding its window and temperature fixed to seek a faster fully resolved method and measure how the critical pair responds to slope.
The 6-minute gradient retains full resolution with a minimum R of 2.46. Test the next shorter gradient to reduce elution time while checking whether the first pair remains above R = 1.5.

The 4-minute gradient achieves maximum CRF, but the first pair is close to the resolution threshold. Raise temperature while keeping the gradient fixed to test whether faster elution and favorable selectivity can preserve full resolution.

Higher temperature worsened the critical early pair, so test the lowest temperature to improve its selectivity while shortening the gradient to the minimum duration. This probes whether temperature can compensate for the resolution lost to a steeper gradient.

Narrow the solvent window to make the 2-minute gradient shallower and improve the early pair’s R from 1.23 toward full resolution. Keep the low temperature that favors this pair, with a strong final solvent to elute the last compound during a short hold.

Shift the successful 0.70-wide gradient upward while keeping slope and temperature fixed to accelerate the last peak. Check whether the stronger starting solvent preserves R ≥ 1.5 for the critical early pair.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to shorten the elution window while slightly reducing gradient steepness. Monitor the early pair for loss of retention; injection 7 remains the fastest fully resolved method tested.

Increase temperature by one grid step to shorten late retention while testing the early pair’s remaining resolution margin. Injection 8 provides a maximum-CRF fallback if the early pair drops below R = 1.5.

Test one higher starting organic fraction to shorten late elution and reduce gradient steepness. The first peak is already close to the unretained region, so this run checks whether early compression outweighs the shallower gradient’s resolution benefit.

Return to the retained starting condition and test the next temperature step to establish the fastest fully resolved temperature boundary. The early pair may fall below R = 1.5; injection 9 remains the fastest maximum-CRF method tested.

Reduce the final organic fraction one step to make the gradient shallower and test whether the early pair recovers full resolution at 35 C. This probes the trade-off between improved early separation and delayed elution of the last compound.

Test whether cooling to 25 C restores the early pair at the higher starting organic fraction that failed at 30 C. This completes a nearby selectivity boundary check while retaining injection 9 as the fastest tested maximum-CRF method.

Lower the starting fraction to keep the early pair within the gradient, while preserving the slope of injection 9 by lowering the endpoint equally. This tests a potentially less retention-sensitive maximum-CRF alternative, although the last peak may elute slightly later.

Combine the best early-pair temperature with a slightly shallower gradient to increase the resolution margin while retaining a short run. The maximum CRF is already achieved; this tests a nearby alternative with potentially more separation margin than injection 9.

Shift injection 15’s solvent window downward at unchanged slope to retain the early peaks more strongly and test their separation margin. This should remain a short maximum-CRF alternative, although the weaker endpoint will delay the last peak.

Test the intermediate temperature between injection 15’s full separation and injection 12’s early-pair failure. This should shorten injection 15 while preserving maximum CRF and checks a neighboring endpoint around the fastest successful method, injection 9.

Cool injection 14 by one step to improve its marginal early-pair resolution while keeping both early peaks away from the unretained region. This tests a short, maximum-CRF alternative with more separation margin; injection 9 remains the fastest fully resolved method tested.

Lower the starting organic fraction relative to injection 7 to retain the early peaks farther from the solvent front while keeping the strongest endpoint for rapid late elution. Test whether the early pair still reaches R = 1.5 despite the slightly steeper gradient.

Test the remaining immediate starting-solvent neighbor of the fastest maximum-CRF method, injection 9. This checks whether stronger early retention can preserve full resolution at 30 C with the fastest endpoint.

Make injection 19’s gradient one step shallower to improve its borderline early-pair resolution while maintaining strong initial retention. This targets another short maximum-CRF method; injection 9 remains the fastest fully resolved option tested.

Raise injection 16’s temperature one step to shorten its late-peak hold while using its early-pair resolution margin to preserve maximum CRF. Injection 9 remains the fastest fully resolved method tested.

Shift the starting fraction of injection 22 upward one step to shorten late elution while testing whether the shallower gradient preserves its early-pair margin. The campaign has already reached maximum CRF; injection 9 remains the fastest fully resolved method tested.

Cool injection 23 one step to increase the critical early-pair resolution margin while retaining a short run and targeting maximum CRF. Injection 9 remains the fastest fully resolved method tested, with its immediate faster neighbors failing resolution.

Use the final injection to test a nearby short method expected to preserve full resolution with stronger early retention than injection 24. Maximum CRF is already secured; injection 9 remains the fastest fully resolved method tested at 2.58 minutes to the last peak.
